title: Best Decentralised Social Media Platforms 2026: DeHub vs Bluesky, Farcaster, Lens & Mastodon
html:
Looking for the best decentralized social media platforms in 2026? The strongest options right now are Bluesky (the biggest, most mainstream network), Mastodon and the wider fediverse (open, non-profit, no ads), Farcaster and Lens (protocol-first, developer-led, and both under new ownership since January), and DeHub, the decentralised social network built from the ground up around a token economy — sixteen native ways to earn, from tradable subscription NFTs and paid DMs to pay-per-view, token-gated posts and up to 90% ad-revenue share.

Most comparison articles stop at "who owns your account". That is the easy half. The two questions that actually decide where a creator should build are: do you get paid here, and who decides what comes down? Almost every network in this list answers the first with "no" and the second with "we do, from our head office". This guide compares on those two axes, covers each platform fairly — including where DeHub is smaller and newer — and looks honestly at what went wrong for the networks that raised the most money. If you want the underlying concepts first, start with decentralised social media explained for UK users.

What "decentralised social media" actually means in 2026

Before the rankings, a quick definition, because the label gets stretched. A genuinely decentralised social network removes the single point of control that defines platforms like Instagram, X and TikTok. In practice that shows up in four ways:

  • Ownership of identity and audience. Your account, your followers and your content are not held hostage by one company that can delete or shadow-ban them at will.
  • Open protocols or open source. The rules of the network are inspectable and, ideally, forkable — anyone can build a client or run a server.
  • Transparent distribution. Reach is determined by a published, chronological or community-driven system rather than a black-box engagement algorithm.
  • Moderation you can see and appeal. Someone still has to take down the illegal and the abusive. The question is whether that power sits with an unnamed trust-and-safety team, or with a process you can inspect, vote in, and appeal to.

Most platforms nail one or two. Several are decentralised in architecture but still behave like a walled garden in practice — the protocol is open, the client everyone actually uses is not. And a smaller group adds a fifth pillar — native creator monetisation — where the network is designed so that attention flows value back to the people who make the content.

That last pillar is where the field thins out dramatically. Pillar four thins it out even further: almost nobody has built moderation into the economics of the network rather than bolting a moderation department onto the side of it. Those two gaps are where DeHub, the decentralised social network, concentrates.

One housekeeping note before we start: the DeHub covered here is the Web3 social platform at dehub.io. It is unrelated to DePaul University's "DeHUB" student portal or Rowan University's "DEHub" digital engineering hub — same-sounding names, completely different things.

First, the honest part: what went wrong for everyone else

It is worth studying the failures before the features, because 2026 was a brutal year for Web3 social and the lessons are specific.

Farcaster raised the most and sold anyway. Farcaster's parent, Merkle Manufactory, raised around US$150 million from Paradigm and a16z at a reported US$1 billion valuation. In January 2026 the infrastructure company Neynar acquired the protocol outright, co-founders Dan Romero and Varun Srinivasan stepped back from day-to-day development, and Merkle moved to return the full US$180 million it had raised to investors. Seven months later, Neynar itself was publicly looking for a new operator for Farcaster and Clanker. The revenue line explains why: roughly US$35.4 million of gross protocol revenue in the first quarter of 2026, against roughly US$377,000 between 1 July and 17 August. That is not a dip, it is a floor falling out.

Farcaster also asked for a bank card at the door. For most of its growth period you could not simply sign up. The dominant client charged around US$5 as an in-app purchase through Apple or Google, or wanted a US phone number, or an existing user paying about US$3 for your invite — a deliberate anti-bot design, and a payment method standing between you and a "permissionless" network. Free registration arrived later, after the growth curve had already been shaped by it.

And it still moderated like a Web2 company. The protocol was open; the app almost everyone used was one company's product, with one company's moderation policy applied from one company's head office. "Sufficiently decentralised" identity does not help you when the client with the users decides your post does not belong there. That pattern repeats across this entire category.

Lens changed hands in the same month. Lens Protocol — the purest "you own your social graph" design in the space — was taken over by Mask Network in January 2026, with a stated goal of building "products people actually use". Its onboarding had already collapsed from tens of thousands of new profiles a day at the 2024 peak to roughly a hundred and fifty, with daily actives falling from around forty-two thousand to single-digit thousands.

Bluesky grew the audience and skipped the business model. Tens of millions of accounts, and as of 2026 still no creator fund, no ad-revenue share, no native tipping and no shipped subscriptions. The company has been explicit that advertising is "not what we believe in". That is a coherent position — it just means every Bluesky creator monetises somewhere else, on Patreon or a newsletter or a brand deal, which is precisely the dependency they left Big Tech to escape.

Mastodon never tried, on principle. No monetisation, by design, and no plan to add it. Worth respecting, and worth being clear-eyed about: your instance admin is still a landlord who can delete your account, and the only money in the system flows to server operators as donations.

The pattern: the networks that decentralised ownership forgot the economy, and the networks that decentralised the social graph forgot the users. Meanwhile, none of them made moderation part of the design. It stayed a cost centre run by staff — the exact thing everyone said they were leaving.

The best decentralized social media platforms 2026, compared

Here is the state of play, platform by platform. User figures are approximate ranges drawn from mid-2026 third-party estimates; every network reports metrics differently, so treat them as orders of magnitude, not precise counts.

Bluesky — the mainstream leader

Bluesky is the closest thing the space has to a household name and, for most people, the easiest decentralized twitter alternative to adopt. Built on the open AT Protocol, it had grown to tens of millions of registered accounts by 2026 — well north of forty million — with monthly active users estimated in the low-to-mid tens of millions. It feels familiar because it is deliberately Twitter-shaped: short posts, follows, reposts, quote posts, and a chronological "Following" feed alongside custom feeds you can choose or build.

The genuinely good parts: account portability is real, you can host your own data, custom feeds put algorithmic control in users' hands, and moderation is composable rather than dictated from one head office. If your only goal is to escape a single owner and keep a large, active audience, Bluesky is the safest bet in 2026.

The honest limitation: there is no native token and no built-in way for creators to earn. Subscriptions have been discussed since 2025 and have not landed; there is no creator fund, no ad-revenue share and no native tipping. It is a better public square, not a creator business. And in practice one company still hosts the overwhelming majority of the network, which is a long way from the on-chain guarantees a social media that pays creators needs.

Best for: writers, journalists, communities and anyone who wants a big, mainstream, decentralised feed without thinking about crypto.

Mastodon and the fediverse — open, non-profit, no monetisation

Mastodon is the elder statesman of decentralised social. It is open-source software run as a non-profit, structured as thousands of independent servers ("instances") that interoperate over the ActivityPub protocol — the fediverse. By 2026 Mastodon itself sits at roughly three-quarters of a million to one million monthly active users, part of a broader fediverse (Pixelfed, PeerTube and others) that has surpassed eleven million total accounts with perhaps one to two million active across all of it.

What Mastodon does brilliantly is community governance and the absence of commercial incentives. There is no algorithm optimising for outrage, no advertising, and no company that can be acquired and enshittified. For many users that is precisely the point.

The trade-offs are the mirror image of that strength. There is no monetisation at all, by design — and there is no content ownership primitive either, so your posts live at the pleasure of whoever runs your instance. Onboarding also asks a bit more of newcomers, since you pick a server before you can start.

Best for: communities, hobbyists and privacy-minded users who want a calm, ad-free, non-commercial home and do not care about earning.

Farcaster — well built, well funded, and sold

Farcaster earned its reputation honestly. "Frames" — interactive mini-apps embedded directly in posts — were the most genuinely new idea in Web3 social for years, the engineering was strong, and the flagship client was polished. Identity and the social graph live on-chain while content sits on off-chain hubs, an approach the team called "sufficient decentralisation".

The 2026 reality check is the ownership story above: acquired by Neynar in January, founders stepped back, US$180 million returned to investors, a new operator sought by August, and gross protocol revenue collapsing from roughly US$35.4 million in Q1 to roughly US$377,000 across seven weeks of the summer. Daily actives have hovered in the tens of thousands — around sixty thousand at recent counts, down from earlier peaks. The culture and vocabulary are also unapologetically crypto-native, which is a feature for insiders and a barrier for everyone else.

Best for: Web3 builders and crypto-natives who want to experiment with on-chain social apps and Frames, and who are comfortable building on a protocol whose operator is currently an open question.

Lens — a social graph as infrastructure

Lens (now running as Lens Protocol on its own chain) takes the most infrastructural approach: it treats your profile, follows and posts as on-chain assets — often as NFTs — that any application can plug into. The pitch is that you own your social graph as portable data and carry it between any Lens-powered app. It is arguably the purest expression of that idea and a serious piece of developer infrastructure.

Adoption remains modest: total accounts number in the hundreds of thousands (around 650,000), with daily active users generally estimated in the low tens of thousands across all clients, and stewardship passed to Mask Network in January 2026. Taken together, neither Lens nor Farcaster had cracked sustained six-figure daily usage by 2026 despite more than a combined US$240 million in funding — a useful reminder that decentralised architecture alone does not summon an audience, and a token that only exists for gas does not make an economy.

Best for: developers building social apps, and users who prioritise owning a portable, composable social graph above reach.

The rest — Minds, Hive, Nostr

Three more deserve a mention:

  • Nostr is not a platform but a radically simple, censorship-resistant protocol built around cryptographic keys and relays. It is beloved by Bitcoiners, supports "zaps" (Bitcoin Lightning tips), and is genuinely hard to censor — but it is technical, fragmented across clients, and small.
  • Minds is an open-source network that has offered crypto-based rewards and boosts for years. It is a legitimate option for creators wanting some token upside, though its reach is limited.
  • Hive is a blockchain-based platform where posts can earn the native token through community voting. It has a dedicated base and real on-chain rewards, but its rewards model is idiosyncratic and its audience is niche.

All three prove that "decentralised" and "pays something" can coexist. None of them combines mainstream-grade media features — video, live streaming, subscriptions, messaging — with creator payouts at any scale.

DeHub — the one built as an economy, not a feed

This is the intersection almost no one else occupies: a full-featured, media-first social network that is decentralised and designed from the first line of code so that every interaction can carry value. That is the entire design premise of DeHub, the decentralised social network — and it is why the feature list below reads like a business rather than an app.

Content can be minted on-chain, so ownership is provable and yours from the moment you mint rather than licensed away in a terms-of-service you never read. Minting is optional: a post publishes instantly off-chain with no wallet, no signature and no gas, and can be minted later from the post itself. The feed is chronological and transparent. And there is no bank card at the door — sign up with socials, email or SMS and gas is sponsored for you, which is the exact opposite of charging US$5 through an app store for the privilege of joining a permissionless network.

Sixteen ways to get paid

Most "Web3 social" platforms have one monetisation mechanic, usually tipping. DeHub has a stack, and each layer is designed to work with the others.

  1. Tips on every post and every live stream, with animated tiers on stream — at a 10% fee, against the roughly 60% the likes of TikTok take on gifting. That single number is the whole thesis in miniature.
  2. Pay-per-view. Charge a one-time unlock on any upload or live stream, priced in any supported token. The creator is paid on unlock, not thirty days later.
  3. Token-gated content. Lock a post behind "hold N of token X" — your own token, DHB, or any supported asset. Anyone can satisfy it by acquiring the token, which turns your content into demand for it.
  4. Subscriber-gated posts. Tie a post to your subscription plan so only your paying members see it.
  5. Tradable subscription NFTs. DeHub was the first protocol to ship fully on-chain subscriptions. A subscription is minted as an NFT the buyer actually owns — so it can be resold on a secondary market, and you take a royalty on every resale, forever. A fan who backed you early holds an asset that appreciates with you rather than a receipt that expires. No Patreon, Substack, OnlyFans or Web2 platform offers this, because it cannot be done without on-chain ownership.
  6. Tier-based communities. Each subscription tier gets its own group chat, perks, early access and private streams, with subscriber analytics behind it.
  7. Paid DMs. Set a per-message fee and your inbox becomes a revenue line instead of a chore. The fee settles on-chain before the message sends, and you keep a free-access list for the people who should always reach you for nothing. Brands, fans and collaborators pay for your attention; time-wasters self-filter.
  8. Watch2Earn bounties. Strap a reward to a post and pay viewers for their attention — first-come or custom distribution. Advertising, but the budget goes to the audience instead of an ad network.
  9. Bounty Hunting. A native, escrowed task market in DHB or USDC across Social Media, Clipping and Contracts. Anyone can post a bounty, anyone can hunt one, the reward is held in escrow from the moment it is posted, and a dispute flow settles disagreements. Creators use it to buy clips and shares; the ecosystem uses it to grow itself.
  10. Up to 90% ad-revenue share, and it is eternal — a post keeps earning ad revenue for life, with no ongoing effort and no platform dependency. Your position on the tips, views and subscriber leaderboards determines your share.
  11. Fractionalised content. Mint a post and it becomes an ERC-1155 split into exactly 1,000 tradeable fractions. Sell some, keep some, gift some to your top supporters — holders then earn proportionally from everything that post ever earns. It is the first model where a fan can genuinely invest in a creator's career and where a creator can raise production budget from their own audience instead of a brand.
  12. Stores. A native storefront on its own page, priced and settled in DHB through the built-in wallet, sitting right next to your content — no external checkout, no redirect, no lost customers.
  13. Live shopping. Sell during the stream, in the stream.
  14. Affiliate and referrals. 20% of the activity of everyone you refer, plus 5% recurring from the people they refer, paid in DHB, tracked end to end in an affiliate dashboard.
  15. Badges. Thirteen tiers, priced in dollars rather than a fixed token count. Each tier cuts your fee on tips, pay-per-views, subscriptions and bounties by a further 0.69%, raises your free daily posting allowance, gives a 5% to 30% discount when buying DHB, and adds weight to every view and reaction you give. Badges can also be lent — one delegation slot per rung climbed — so influence travels with a crew instead of sitting on one wallet.
  16. Moderation mining. Yes, moderating pays. See below, because this is the part nobody else built.

On top of that sit staking with thirteen tiers of SuperPowers, a play-to-earn arcade including the flagship battle-royale "Last Chad Standing", username and account marketplaces, and an AI creator suite — assistant, agents, image, video, music and poster generation — with no external accounts or API keys. Sending tokens to another user is always free; fees only exist on the premium rails above.

Decentralised moderation — the part nobody else thought to build

Every other network in this guide treats moderation as an expense: hire a trust-and-safety team, publish a policy, absorb the appeals. DeHub treats it as a market, wired directly into the token economy. It is the single most distinctive thing about the platform and the hardest for any competitor to copy, because it only works if your network already has an economy running through it.

Here is how it works:

  • Stake to moderate. $DHB can be staked into moderation pools. Flagged content enters a queue, stakers vote on the outcome — remove, warn, ignore — and correct votes earn rewards while wrong votes get slashed. Skin in the game, priced.
  • Quadratic voting, so whales cannot buy verdicts. Voting power is the square root of tokens staked: 100 staked is 10 votes, 10,000 staked is 100 votes, not 10,000. More tokens means more influence; it never means unchecked power.
  • Moderation mining. When a post is removed, the ad revenue and play-to-earn bounties attached to it are shared across every wallet that voted. Keeping the network clean is a paid job open to anyone, which is exactly why bad actors find it expensive and honest users find it worth turning up for.
  • Delegated moderation. Do not want to vote on everything? Delegate to a curator or a moderation pool the way you would stake to a validator, and swap them whenever you like. Passive users still participate; active ones get rewarded.
  • Curation markets. Stake to boost content you believe in. Boost something that later gets flagged and you can be slashed for it — so promotion carries responsibility instead of being free reach.
  • DAO appeals. A creator can appeal a decision as a DAO proposal, voted on with the same quadratic logic, which is the structural defence against moderation cartels and brigading. Appeals are also tracked in-app as real tickets with a reference number and an answer that comes back — not an email address that goes nowhere.
  • Progressive caps and sybil resistance. Influence decays past certain staking thresholds to encourage wider distribution, and key votes require both stake and reputation.
  • Every decision logged on-chain. A transparent, permanent moderation history. You can audit why something came down. Try that on any Big Tech platform, or on the dominant client of any other network in this list.

Two honest clarifications. First, genuinely illegal or harmful content does not wait for a vote: community-elected administrators and top-tier badge holders hold delegated takedown rights and act immediately, with policy set by governance and every action appealable. Second, decentralised does not mean unfiltered — per-post content ratings keep adult material off the public feed while letting it exist on the platform, so nobody's timeline becomes someone else's problem.

That combination — economic incentives, quadratic voting, slashing, delegation, DAO appeals and an on-chain record — is a governance system, not a moderation department. It is what "prevents centralized censorship while maintaining quality standards" actually looks like when you build it in rather than bolt it on.

Built in the open, shipped daily

Two of the five networks in this guide changed owners in January 2026 and one of them was looking for another operator by August. So it is fair to ask who is still building.

DeHub's lead developer, mal.eth, sits at #34 on the public ghcommits.com all-time GitHub commits leaderboard with more than 19,000 commits — a public, independently tracked, verifiable record of shipping, not a roadmap slide. The platform ships to web, Android and iOS from the same codebase, with a custom CDN running sub-200ms globally, DePIN infrastructure, open-source end-to-end encrypted messaging (XChaCha20-Poly1305, X25519 ECDH), and live streaming on Livepeer that has scaled past 50,000 concurrent viewers.

The ecosystem runs on the DHB token ($DHB), primarily on Base (an Ethereum Layer 2), with contracts also on BNB Chain, Polygon and Solana addresses on every account. DeHub is an independent DAO governed by its token holders, and its co-founders, Mike Hales and Indi Jay Cammish, also founded First Class Agency — the UK's number-one official TikTok LIVE partner agency — so the team has run creator monetisation at scale from the inside.

Now the honest part, because this comparison is only useful if it is fair: DeHub is newer and smaller than Bluesky. If your single priority is the largest possible mainstream audience today, Bluesky wins on raw scale. DeHub's bet is different — that creators follow the platform that pays them, and that a network with sixteen revenue rails and a moderation system that pays its own participants has a business where the others have a hobby.

Best for: creators and communities who want to own their content, keep their audience, and earn from video, live streams, subscriptions, messages, storefronts and attention — not just post into a void.

Monetisation, side by side

Fourteen earning mechanics, and which of the five networks actually has them. "Partial" means it exists through third-party apps or modules rather than as a native feature.

  • Native tips — DeHub: yes, at a 10% fee. Bluesky: no. Mastodon: no. Farcaster: partial, through apps. Lens: partial, through collect modules.
  • Pay-per-view unlocks — DeHub: yes. Bluesky: no. Mastodon: no. Farcaster: no. Lens: partial.
  • Token-gated content — DeHub: yes. Bluesky: no. Mastodon: no. Farcaster: no. Lens: partial.
  • Creator subscriptions — DeHub: yes, fully on-chain. Bluesky: announced, never shipped. Mastodon, Farcaster and Lens: no.
  • Resellable subscriptions that pay the creator a royalty — DeHub only. No other network in this guide has it, and neither does any Web2 subscription platform.
  • Paid DMs — DeHub only.
  • Paying viewers for their attention — DeHub only.
  • Escrowed bounty marketplace — DeHub only.
  • Ad-revenue share to creators — DeHub: up to 90%, for the life of the post. Bluesky and Mastodon: no advertising at all, so nothing to share. Farcaster and Lens: no.
  • Fans buying a stake in a post — DeHub only, via 1,000 tradeable fractions per upload.
  • Native storefront and live shopping — DeHub only.
  • Affiliate programme — DeHub: 20%, plus 5% recurring on second-tier referrals. Everyone else: none.
  • Fee discounts for token holders — DeHub: thirteen badge tiers. Farcaster and Lens: no. Bluesky and Mastodon: no fees to discount, because there is nothing to earn.
  • Paid moderation — DeHub only.

How to choose the best decentralised social media for you

Skip the leaderboard mindset. The "best" platform is the one that matches your actual use case.

If you want the biggest mainstream audience

Choose Bluesky. It has the scale, the familiar interface and the lowest barrier to entry. Accept that you are there for reach and conversation, not income, and that you will still be monetising somewhere else.

If you want a calm, non-commercial, ad-free community

Choose Mastodon or another fediverse platform. You get genuine community governance and zero advertising. Accept that there is no monetisation, no content ownership, and an instance admin who can still switch you off.

If you are a developer or crypto-native experimenter

Choose Farcaster or Lens. You get on-chain identity, composability and a builder culture. Accept that daily active audiences are small, the vocabulary is insider-heavy, and both protocols are under new stewardship as of 2026.

If you want to get paid for your content

Choose DeHub. It is the only option in this guide where video, live streams, subscriptions, messages, storefronts, referrals and viewer attention all generate on-chain income, where subscriptions are assets your fans can trade and you keep earning royalties on, and where moderation itself pays. Accept that it is younger and smaller than Bluesky — and decide whether ownership, earnings and a say in the rules matter more to you than sheer headcount.

If you are specifically leaving TikTok

Read the UK creator's guide to leaving TikTok first. Short-form creators have particular needs — video-first tooling, live streaming and payouts — and the right destination is rarely a text-first network. This is precisely the gap DeHub is built to fill.

The pattern to notice

Line the platforms up and a three-way split appears. On one side sit the networks that decentralise ownership and speech — Bluesky, Mastodon, and to a degree Nostr — but leave creator earnings off the table and keep moderation in-house. On the other sit the networks that decentralise the social graph as infrastructure — Farcaster and Lens — brilliant for builders, small in practice, and both sold or handed over within a single month of 2026.

DeHub is deliberately built across a third axis: decentralised ownership plus mainstream media features plus an entire economy — sixteen ways to earn, a subscription that is an asset rather than a receipt, an inbox with a price on it, and a moderation system that pays the people who run it.

No single platform is objectively "the best". But if the most valuable things a creator has are their audience and their output, the interesting question in 2026 is not "which network is the biggest?" It is "which network lets me own both, earn from both, and vote on the rules that govern them?" On that question, the field narrows to one.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best decentralized social media platform in 2026?

There is no single winner — it depends on your goal. For the biggest mainstream audience, Bluesky leads with tens of millions of users. For a calm, ad-free community, Mastodon and the fediverse are strongest. For developers and crypto-natives, Farcaster and Lens are the most interesting, though both changed ownership in January 2026. For creators who want to actually earn — through tradable subscriptions, paid DMs, pay-per-view, gated content, watch-to-earn and ad-revenue share — DeHub is purpose-built for that, though it is newer and smaller than Bluesky.

Which decentralised social network pays creators the most?

DeHub, by a distance, because it is not one mechanic but sixteen: tips at a 10% fee, pay-per-view unlocks, token-gated and subscriber-only posts, on-chain subscription NFTs your fans can resell while you keep the royalty, paid DMs, watch-to-earn bounties, an escrowed bounty marketplace, up to 90% ad-revenue share that keeps paying for the life of the post, fractional ownership of content, native stores and live shopping, a 20% affiliate programme, fee discounts across thirteen badge tiers, and paid moderation. Bluesky and Mastodon do not pay creators natively at all; Hive and Minds offer smaller on-chain rewards. Earnings always depend on your audience and engagement, so treat any platform's payout mechanics as opportunity, not a guarantee.

What are tradable subscriptions?

A normal subscription is a receipt — you pay, you get access, it expires, and it is worth nothing to anyone else. On DeHub a subscription is minted as an NFT the subscriber actually owns, so it can be sold on to someone else, and the creator takes a royalty on that resale and every resale after it. For fans it turns support into a potential asset; for creators it adds a secondary income stream on top of the original sale. No Web2 subscription platform can offer it, because it requires on-chain ownership to exist.

Can you charge people to message you?

On DeHub, yes. Creators set a per-message fee, paid on-chain before the message is delivered, and keep a free-access list for the people who should always reach them for nothing. It turns an inbox from an unpaid support desk into a revenue line, and it filters time-wasters automatically. No other network in this comparison has it.

Who moderates a decentralised social network?

On most of them, a company — the protocol may be open, but the client the users are on applies one organisation's policy. DeHub is the exception: moderation runs on staked $DHB with quadratic voting, correct votes earn and wrong votes are slashed, the ad revenue and bounties of removed content are shared among everyone who voted, appeals go to the DAO, and every decision is logged on-chain. Elected admins and top badge holders can still remove illegal or harmful content immediately, under policy governance sets and with an appeal attached.

Is Bluesky better than DeHub?

They optimise for different things. Bluesky is bigger and more mainstream, and it is the easier pick if you simply want a large, familiar, decentralised text feed. DeHub is media-first and built to pay creators, with video, live streaming, subscriptions, paid messaging and on-chain ownership — but it is younger and has a smaller audience today. If reach is your priority, Bluesky; if ownership and income are, DeHub.

Are decentralised social media platforms actually safe and legit?

The established ones are legitimate technologies, not scams — Bluesky, Mastodon, Farcaster, Lens and DeHub are all real, working networks, several of them open source and inspectable. As with any platform, do your own diligence: read how monetisation works, understand that token-based rewards carry market risk, and never treat crypto earnings as guaranteed income. Open-source code and on-chain transparency make the credible projects easier to verify than closed Big Tech alternatives.

Do I need cryptocurrency to use a decentralised social network?

Not usually to browse or post. Bluesky and Mastodon involve no crypto at all. On DeHub you can sign up with socials, email or SMS with gas sponsored for you, browse freely and post inside a daily allowance — no card, no seed phrase, no KYC. Earning, tokenised uploads, subscriptions and tips involve the DHB token, which you can top up in two clicks when you are ready.

What is the best decentralized Twitter alternative?

For a like-for-like Twitter replacement — short posts, a familiar feed, a large audience — Bluesky is the strongest decentralized twitter alternative in 2026. If you want a Twitter-style experience that also lets you earn from your content, own it on-chain and vote on the rules, DeHub is the creator-focused alternative worth trying alongside it.

Try a decentralised network that pays you

The fastest way to understand the difference is to use one. Explore the feed, tokenise an upload, put a price on your inbox, or go live at dehub.io, open the DeHub app in your browser, or download it on Google Play. Own your content, keep your audience, and get paid for the attention you already create.

- **Open protocols or open source.** The rules of the network are inspectable and, ideally, forkable — anyone can build a client or run a server.
- **Transparent distribution.** Reach is determined by a published, chronological or community-driven system rather than a black-box engagement algorithm.
- **Moderation you can see and appeal.** Someone still has to take down the illegal and the abusive. The question is whether that power sits with an unnamed trust-and-safety team, or with a process you can inspect, vote in, and appeal to.

Most platforms nail one or two. Several are decentralised in architecture but still behave like a walled garden in practice — the protocol is open, the client everyone actually uses is not. And a smaller group adds a fifth pillar — **native creator monetisation** — where the network is designed so that attention flows value back to the people who make the content.

That last pillar is where the field thins out dramatically. Pillar four thins it out even further: almost nobody has built moderation into the economics of the network rather than bolting a moderation department onto the side of it. Those two gaps are where DeHub, the decentralised social network, concentrates.

## First, the honest part: what went wrong for everyone else

It is worth studying the failures before the features, because 2026 was a brutal year for Web3 social and the lessons are specific.

**Farcaster raised the most and sold anyway.** Farcaster's parent, Merkle Manufactory, raised around US$150 million from Paradigm and a16z at a reported US$1 billion valuation. In January 2026 the infrastructure company Neynar [acquired the protocol outright](https://neynar.com/blog/neynar-is-acquiring-farcaster), co-founders Dan Romero and Varun Srinivasan [stepped back from day-to-day development](https://www.coindesk.com/business/2026/01/21/farcaster-founders-step-back-as-neynar-acquires-struggling-crypto-social-app), and Merkle moved to return the full US$180 million it had raised to investors. Seven months later, Neynar itself was [publicly looking for a new operator](https://crypto.news/farcaster-seeks-new-operator-seven-months-after-sale/) for Farcaster and Clanker. The revenue line explains why: roughly US$35.4 million of gross protocol revenue in the first quarter of 2026, against roughly US$377,000 between 1 July and 17 August. That is not a dip, it is a floor falling out.

**Farcaster also asked for a bank card at the door.** For most of its growth period you could not simply sign up. The dominant client charged around US$5 as an in-app purchase through Apple or Google, or wanted a US phone number, or an existing user paying about US$3 for your invite — [a deliberate anti-bot design](https://techcrunch.com/2024/02/06/farcaster-decentralized-social-network-mass-adoption/), and a payment method standing between you and a "permissionless" network. Free registration arrived later, after the growth curve had already been shaped by it.

**And it still moderated like a Web2 company.** The protocol was open; the app almost everyone used was one company's product, with one company's moderation policy applied from one company's head office. "Sufficiently decentralised" identity does not help you when the client with the users decides your post does not belong there. That pattern repeats across this entire category.

**Lens changed hands in the same month.** Lens Protocol — the purest "you own your social graph" design in the space — was [taken over by Mask Network in January 2026](https://www.theblock.co/post/386293/mask-network-takes-over-lens-protocol-with-goal-to-build-products-people-actually-use), with a stated goal of building "products people actually use". Its onboarding had already collapsed from tens of thousands of new profiles a day at the 2024 peak to roughly a hundred and fifty, with daily actives falling from around forty-two thousand to single-digit thousands.

**Bluesky grew the audience and skipped the business model.** Tens of millions of accounts, and as of 2026 still no creator fund, no ad-revenue share, no native tipping and no shipped subscriptions. The company has been explicit that advertising is "not what we believe in". That is a coherent position — it just means every Bluesky creator monetises somewhere else, on Patreon or a newsletter or a brand deal, which is precisely the dependency they left Big Tech to escape.

**Mastodon never tried, on principle.** No monetisation, by design, and no plan to add it. Worth respecting, and worth being clear-eyed about: your instance admin is still a landlord who can delete your account, and the only money in the system flows to server operators as donations.

The pattern: the networks that decentralised **ownership** forgot the **economy**, and the networks that decentralised the **social graph** forgot the **users**. Meanwhile, none of them made moderation part of the design. It stayed a cost centre run by staff — the exact thing everyone said they were leaving.

## The best decentralized social media platforms 2026, compared

Here is the state of play, platform by platform. User figures are approximate ranges drawn from mid-2026 third-party estimates; every network reports metrics differently, so treat them as orders of magnitude, not precise counts.

### Bluesky — the mainstream leader

Bluesky is the closest thing the space has to a household name and, for most people, the easiest **decentralized twitter alternative** to adopt. Built on the open AT Protocol, it had grown to tens of millions of registered accounts by 2026 — well north of forty million — with monthly active users estimated in the low-to-mid tens of millions. It feels familiar because it is deliberately Twitter-shaped: short posts, follows, reposts, quote posts, and a chronological "Following" feed alongside custom feeds you can choose or build.

The genuinely good parts: account portability is real, you can host your own data, custom feeds put algorithmic control in users' hands, and moderation is composable rather than dictated from one head office. If your only goal is to escape a single owner and keep a large, active audience, Bluesky is the safest bet in 2026.

The honest limitation: **there is no native token and no built-in way for creators to earn.** Subscriptions have been discussed since 2025 and have not landed; there is no creator fund, no ad-revenue share and no native tipping. It is a better public square, not a creator business. And in practice one company still hosts the overwhelming majority of the network, which is a long way from the on-chain guarantees a **social media that pays creators** needs.

**Best for:** writers, journalists, communities and anyone who wants a big, mainstream, decentralised feed without thinking about crypto.

### Mastodon and the fediverse — open, non-profit, no monetisation

Mastodon is the elder statesman of decentralised social. It is open-source software run as a non-profit, structured as thousands of independent servers ("instances") that interoperate over the ActivityPub protocol — the fediverse. By 2026 Mastodon itself sits at roughly three-quarters of a million to one million monthly active users, part of a broader fediverse (Pixelfed, PeerTube and others) that has surpassed eleven million total accounts with perhaps one to two million active across all of it.

What Mastodon does brilliantly is community governance and the absence of commercial incentives. There is no algorithm optimising for outrage, no advertising, and no company that can be acquired and enshittified. For many users that is precisely the point.

The trade-offs are the mirror image of that strength. **There is no monetisation at all, by design** — and there is no content ownership primitive either, so your posts live at the pleasure of whoever runs your instance. Onboarding also asks a bit more of newcomers, since you pick a server before you can start.

**Best for:** communities, hobbyists and privacy-minded users who want a calm, ad-free, non-commercial home and do not care about earning.

### Farcaster — well built, well funded, and sold

Farcaster earned its reputation honestly. "Frames" — interactive mini-apps embedded directly in posts — were the most genuinely new idea in Web3 social for years, the engineering was strong, and the flagship client was polished. Identity and the social graph live on-chain while content sits on off-chain hubs, an approach the team called "sufficient decentralisation".

The 2026 reality check is the ownership story above: acquired by Neynar in January, founders stepped back, US$180 million returned to investors, a new operator sought by August, and gross protocol revenue collapsing from roughly US$35.4 million in Q1 to roughly US$377,000 across seven weeks of the summer. Daily actives have hovered in the tens of thousands — around sixty thousand at recent counts, down from earlier peaks. The culture and vocabulary are also unapologetically crypto-native, which is a feature for insiders and a barrier for everyone else.

**Best for:** Web3 builders and crypto-natives who want to experiment with on-chain social apps and Frames, and who are comfortable building on a protocol whose operator is currently an open question.

### Lens — a social graph as infrastructure

Lens (now running as Lens Protocol on its own chain) takes the most infrastructural approach: it treats your profile, follows and posts as on-chain assets — often as NFTs — that any application can plug into. The pitch is that you own your social graph as portable data and carry it between any Lens-powered app. It is arguably the purest expression of that idea and a serious piece of developer infrastructure.

Adoption remains modest: total accounts number in the hundreds of thousands (around 650,000), with daily active users generally estimated in the low tens of thousands across all clients, and stewardship passed to Mask Network in January 2026. Taken together, neither Lens nor Farcaster had cracked sustained six-figure daily usage by 2026 despite more than a combined US$240 million in funding — a useful reminder that decentralised architecture alone does not summon an audience, and a token that only exists for gas does not make an economy.

**Best for:** developers building social apps, and users who prioritise owning a portable, composable social graph above reach.

### The rest — Minds, Hive, Nostr

Three more deserve a mention:

- **Nostr** is not a platform but a radically simple, censorship-resistant protocol built around cryptographic keys and relays. It is beloved by Bitcoiners, supports "zaps" (Bitcoin Lightning tips), and is genuinely hard to censor — but it is technical, fragmented across clients, and small.
- **Minds** is an open-source network that has offered crypto-based rewards and boosts for years. It is a legitimate option for creators wanting some token upside, though its reach is limited.
- **Hive** is a blockchain-based platform where posts can earn the native token through community voting. It has a dedicated base and real on-chain rewards, but its rewards model is idiosyncratic and its audience is niche.

All three prove that "decentralised" and "pays something" can coexist. None of them combines mainstream-grade media features — video, live streaming, subscriptions, messaging — with creator payouts at any scale.

### Decentralised moderation — the part nobody else thought to build

Every other network in this guide treats moderation as an expense: hire a trust-and-safety team, publish a policy, absorb the appeals. DeHub treats it as a market, wired directly into the token economy. It is the single most distinctive thing about the platform and the hardest for any competitor to copy, because it only works if your network already has an economy running through it.

Here is how it works:

- **Stake to moderate.** $DHB can be staked into moderation pools. Flagged content enters a queue, stakers vote on the outcome — remove, warn, ignore — and **correct votes earn rewards while wrong votes get slashed**. Skin in the game, priced.
- **Quadratic voting, so whales cannot buy verdicts.** Voting power is the square root of tokens staked: 100 staked is 10 votes, 10,000 staked is 100 votes, not 10,000. More tokens means more influence; it never means unchecked power.
- **Moderation mining.** When a post is removed, the ad revenue and play-to-earn bounties attached to it are **shared across every wallet that voted**. Keeping the network clean is a paid job open to anyone, which is exactly why bad actors find it expensive and honest users find it worth turning up for.
- **Delegated moderation.** Do not want to vote on everything? Delegate to a curator or a moderation pool the way you would stake to a validator, and swap them whenever you like. Passive users still participate; active ones get rewarded.
- **Curation markets.** Stake to boost content you believe in. Boost something that later gets flagged and you can be slashed for it — so promotion carries responsibility instead of being free reach.
- **DAO appeals.** A creator can appeal a decision as a DAO proposal, voted on with the same quadratic logic, which is the structural defence against moderation cartels and brigading. Appeals are also tracked in-app as real tickets with a reference number and an answer that comes back — not an email address that goes nowhere.
- **Progressive caps and sybil resistance.** Influence decays past certain staking thresholds to encourage wider distribution, and key votes require both stake and reputation.
- **Every decision logged on-chain.** A transparent, permanent moderation history. You can audit why something came down. Try that on any Big Tech platform, or on the dominant client of any other network in this list.

Two honest clarifications. First, genuinely illegal or harmful content does not wait for a vote: community-elected administrators and top-tier badge holders hold delegated takedown rights and act immediately, with policy set by governance and every action appealable. Second, decentralised does not mean unfiltered — per-post content ratings keep adult material off the public feed while letting it exist on the platform, so nobody's timeline becomes someone else's problem.

That combination — economic incentives, quadratic voting, slashing, delegation, DAO appeals and an on-chain record — is a governance system, not a moderation department. It is what "prevents centralized censorship while maintaining quality standards" actually looks like when you build it in rather than bolt it on.

## How to choose the best decentralised social media for you

Skip the leaderboard mindset. The "best" platform is the one that matches your actual use case.

### If you want the biggest mainstream audience

Choose **Bluesky**. It has the scale, the familiar interface and the lowest barrier to entry. Accept that you are there for reach and conversation, not income, and that you will still be monetising somewhere else.

### If you want a calm, non-commercial, ad-free community

Choose **Mastodon** or another fediverse platform. You get genuine community governance and zero advertising. Accept that there is no monetisation, no content ownership, and an instance admin who can still switch you off.

### If you are a developer or crypto-native experimenter

Choose **Farcaster** or **Lens**. You get on-chain identity, composability and a builder culture. Accept that daily active audiences are small, the vocabulary is insider-heavy, and both protocols are under new stewardship as of 2026.

### If you want to get paid for your content

Choose **DeHub**. It is the only option in this guide where video, live streams, subscriptions, messages, storefronts, referrals and viewer attention all generate on-chain income, where subscriptions are assets your fans can trade and you keep earning royalties on, and where moderation itself pays. Accept that it is younger and smaller than Bluesky — and decide whether ownership, earnings and a say in the rules matter more to you than sheer headcount.

### If you are specifically leaving TikTok

Read [the UK creator's guide to leaving TikTok](/guides/uk-creators-guide-leaving-tiktok) first. Short-form creators have particular needs — video-first tooling, live streaming and payouts — and the right destination is rarely a text-first network. This is precisely the gap DeHub is built to fill.

## The pattern to notice

Line the platforms up and a three-way split appears. On one side sit the networks that decentralise **ownership and speech** — Bluesky, Mastodon, and to a degree Nostr — but leave creator earnings off the table and keep moderation in-house. On the other sit the networks that decentralise the **social graph as infrastructure** — Farcaster and Lens — brilliant for builders, small in practice, and both sold or handed over within a single month of 2026.

DeHub is deliberately built across a third axis: decentralised ownership **plus** mainstream media features **plus** an entire economy — sixteen ways to earn, a subscription that is an asset rather than a receipt, an inbox with a price on it, and a moderation system that pays the people who run it.

No single platform is objectively "the best". But if the most valuable things a creator has are their audience and their output, the interesting question in 2026 is not "which network is the biggest?" It is "which network lets me own both, earn from both, and vote on the rules that govern them?" On that question, the field narrows to one.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the best decentralized social media platform in 2026?

There is no single winner — it depends on your goal. For the biggest mainstream audience, Bluesky leads with tens of millions of users. For a calm, ad-free community, Mastodon and the fediverse are strongest. For developers and crypto-natives, Farcaster and Lens are the most interesting, though both changed ownership in January 2026. For creators who want to actually earn — through tradable subscriptions, paid DMs, pay-per-view, gated content, watch-to-earn and ad-revenue share — DeHub is purpose-built for that, though it is newer and smaller than Bluesky.

### Which decentralised social network pays creators the most?

DeHub, by a distance, because it is not one mechanic but sixteen: tips at a 10% fee, pay-per-view unlocks, token-gated and subscriber-only posts, on-chain subscription NFTs your fans can resell while you keep the royalty, paid DMs, watch-to-earn bounties, an escrowed bounty marketplace, up to 90% ad-revenue share that keeps paying for the life of the post, fractional ownership of content, native stores and live shopping, a 20% affiliate programme, fee discounts across thirteen badge tiers, and paid moderation. Earnings always depend on your audience and engagement, so treat any platform's payout mechanics as opportunity, not a guarantee.

### What are tradable subscriptions?

A normal subscription is a receipt — you pay, you get access, it expires, and it is worth nothing to anyone else. On DeHub a subscription is minted as an NFT the subscriber actually owns, so it can be sold on to someone else, and the creator takes a royalty on that resale and every resale after it. For fans it turns support into a potential asset; for creators it adds a secondary income stream on top of the original sale. No Web2 subscription platform can offer it, because it requires on-chain ownership to exist.

### Can you charge people to message you?

On DeHub, yes. Creators set a per-message fee, paid on-chain before the message is delivered, and keep a free-access list for the people who should always reach them for nothing. It turns an inbox from an unpaid support desk into a revenue line, and it filters time-wasters automatically. No other network in this comparison has it.

### Who moderates a decentralised social network?

On most of them, a company — the protocol may be open, but the client the users are on applies one organisation's policy. DeHub is the exception: moderation runs on staked $DHB with quadratic voting, correct votes earn and wrong votes are slashed, the ad revenue and bounties of removed content are shared among everyone who voted, appeals go to the DAO, and every decision is logged on-chain. Elected admins and top badge holders can still remove illegal or harmful content immediately, under policy governance sets and with an appeal attached.

### Is Bluesky better than DeHub?

They optimise for different things. Bluesky is bigger and more mainstream, and it is the easier pick if you simply want a large, familiar, decentralised text feed. DeHub is media-first and built to pay creators, with video, live streaming, subscriptions, paid messaging and on-chain ownership — but it is younger and has a smaller audience today. If reach is your priority, Bluesky; if ownership and income are, DeHub.

### Are decentralised social media platforms actually safe and legit?

The established ones are legitimate technologies, not scams — Bluesky, Mastodon, Farcaster, Lens and DeHub are all real, working networks, several of them open source and inspectable. As with any platform, do your own diligence: read how monetisation works, understand that token-based rewards carry market risk, and never treat crypto earnings as guaranteed income. Open-source code and on-chain transparency make the credible projects easier to verify than closed Big Tech alternatives.

### Do I need cryptocurrency to use a decentralised social network?

Not usually to browse or post. Bluesky and Mastodon involve no crypto at all. On DeHub you can sign up with socials, email or SMS with gas sponsored for you, browse freely and post inside a daily allowance — no card, no seed phrase, no KYC. Earning, tokenised uploads, subscriptions and tips involve the DHB token, which you can top up in two clicks when you are ready.

For a like-for-like Twitter replacement — short posts, a familiar feed, a large audience — Bluesky is the strongest **decentralized twitter alternative** in 2026.
